templates.name: Principle plus case leads to consequence (S10 trade-off folded in)
Rule or timeline plus observation rejects a premise
Undercut leads to a hedged conclusion
X but not Y, so Z
Two cases or two accounts lead to a conditional or a common ground
Co-occurrence or repeated pattern leads to a link
Behaviour, design or content reveals a motive or belief (S12 example folded in)
Received view plus counterevidence leads to revision

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a perception principle applied to a catalog that freezes one viewing angle
items.passage: In Noh, a classical Japanese theatrical tradition, principal roles are often performed in carved wooden masks whose features cannot move, yet accomplished actors can make a single mask appear to convey a considerable range of emotions. Investigating this effect, researcher Michael Lyons and colleagues showed viewers photographs of a Noh mask at various vertical angles: tilted forward, the mask was more often judged happy, and tilted backward, more often judged sad, apparently because viewers misinterpret the changes that tilting produces in a face’s image as movements of its muscles. If that explanation is accurate, a museum catalog that photographs each Noh mask only from directly in front would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: reveal the expression that each mask’s carver intended more faithfully than any stage performance of the mask could.
make each mask seem to change its expression from one photograph to the next, since viewers read changes in a mask’s angle as changes in its features.
show each mask with only one of the several expressions that it can appear to have during a performance.
lead readers to judge most of the masks as sad, since none of the masks would be shown tilted forward.
items.explanation: The text says that “tilted forward, the mask was more often judged happy, and tilted backward, more often judged sad,” which is how accomplished actors “can make a single mask appear to convey a considerable range of emotions.” A catalog that shows each mask “only from directly in front” captures a single angle, so each mask would appear with just one of the expressions it can take on as an actor tilts it onstage, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about what expression a carver intended; it explains only how tilting changes the expression viewers perceive, so it gives no reason to call a frontal photograph more faithful than a performance.

B.recipe: principle applied to the wrong case (MIX)
B.why_wrong: Viewers do read changes in angle as changes in expression, but every photograph in this catalog shows the mask from the same angle, “directly in front,” so nothing would change from one photograph to the next.

D.why_wrong: The masks would not be tilted forward, but they would not be tilted backward either, and the text links sadness to a backward tilt, so there is no basis for expecting readers to judge the masks sad.

sources.what: Lyons, Campbell, Plante, Coleman, Kamachi, Akamatsu 2000, Proc. R. Soc. B, The Noh mask effect: full-face masks worn by skilled Noh actors can induce a variety of perceived expressions with changes in head orientation; out-of-plane rotation changes the 2D image, which viewers may misinterpret as muscle action; a forward tilted mask was more often judged happy, a backward tilted one more often sad (moderated by culture, left out)

items.notes: Area: humanities (theater) with perception research. S2: tilt changes perceived expression, applied to a catalog that shows one angle. Simplified: the cultural moderation (Japanese viewers saw happiness at more backward tilt) is left out; the passage keeps to the overall Experiment 1 result. Distractors: CAUSE (carver's intent), MIX (principle applied though the angle never changes), REV near-miss (no forward tilt read as sad). Review: key paraphrased (one of the several expressions) and A no longer carries a reason clause, so the key is not the only option without one.

fixes: opening reworded (principal roles performed in masks whose features cannot move) so it no longer echoes transitions w2b3_06; Noh judged not a repeat: w2b3_06 contrasts Noh and kyogen staging, this item turns on one perception study (shared art form only, different subject and skill)
“psychologist Michael Lyons” changed to “researcher” (the abstract places Lyons at a telecommunications research lab)
“changes in a face’s outline” changed to “misinterpret the changes that tilting produces in a face’s image” (the source says viewers may misinterpret changes in two-dimensional image characteristics)

read a shade easy (key the only option without a reason clause; “convey the variety” echoed “convey a considerable range”): key paraphrased (only one of the several expressions), A’s reason clause dropped; re-solved, C only
review.note: Noh repeat check: not a repeat of transitions w2b3_06 (see fixes)

band7.why: Two steps (tilting changes the perceived expression; a front-only catalog fixes one angle, so one expression), the account in a long second sentence. B applies the right mechanism to a case with no change of angle, D keeps half the rule (no forward tilt) and drops the other, A a rival claim; key paraphrased. Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: learned migration applied to a herd replaced by newcomers
items.passage: Many hoofed mammals migrate by “surfing” green waves, traveling across a landscape in step with the spring flush of fresh plant growth. To determine whether this behavior is inherited or acquired, ecologist Brett Jesmer and colleagues compared bighorn sheep and moose from populations that had occupied their ranges for centuries with animals that had been translocated into unfamiliar ranges. Whereas most animals in the long-established populations migrated, the translocated animals initially did not, and their populations became more migratory only after several decades. These results suggest that if a migratory herd were wiped out and replaced with animals brought from elsewhere, the new herd would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: need decades to rebuild the knowledge of seasonal forage that the original herd had gathered over many generations.
begin migrating as soon as it arrived, provided that its animals came from herds that migrated in their former ranges.
regain the original herd’s migration within a generation or two, since young animals inherit their parents’ tendency to migrate.
travel farther each spring than the original herd had, since animals in an unfamiliar range must search more widely for food.
items.explanation: Animals “translocated into unfamiliar ranges” did not migrate at first, and their populations became more migratory “only after several decades,” while populations that had occupied their ranges “for centuries” mostly migrated. So migrating depends on knowledge of a particular landscape that builds up slowly, and a replacement herd would need decades to rebuild what the original herd knew, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text gives no exception for animals from migratory herds; it says the translocated animals “initially did not” migrate, which suggests that migrating depends on knowing the new range, not on where the animals came from.

C.why_wrong: If the tendency were simply inherited, the translocated animals would have migrated from the start; instead their populations took “several decades” to become more migratory, which points to learning, not inheritance.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how far animals travel in an unfamiliar range; it reports only that translocated animals initially did not migrate.

sources.what: Jesmer et al. 2018, Science 361:1023: bighorn sheep and moose translocated into novel habitats were initially not migratory, unlike historical populations that persisted for hundreds of years; after multiple decades translocated populations gained knowledge about surfing green waves and increased migration; loss of migration will expunge generations of knowledge about forage

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S2: migration is learned over decades, applied to a herd replaced by newcomers (T3). Distractors: MIX (added condition: source herds migratory), CAUSE (inheritance), CMP (travel farther).

fixes: “much more migratory” changed to “more migratory” (the source says the populations increased their propensity to migrate)

band7.why: Two steps (translocated animals took decades, so migration is learned, not inherited; apply to a replaced herd). B adds a plausible condition, C the inheritance rival the study ruled against, D a CMP; key paraphrased (knowledge of seasonal forage). Band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: an income comparison model applied to a change in what people can see
items.passage: According to income comparison models, individuals evaluate their own well-being partly by comparing their earnings with those of others, so that an identical salary can feel more or less satisfying depending on what neighbors and colleagues earn. Norwegian tax records have long been publicly available, but in 2001 they became easily searchable online, allowing anyone to look up an acquaintance’s income in moments. Consistent with such models, economist Ricardo Perez-Truglia found in national survey data spanning 1985 to 2013 that once the records went online, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Norwegians at every income level reported lower happiness, since nearly everyone could now find someone who earned more.
lower-income Norwegians grew happier, since they could now see how many others earned as little as they did.
Norwegians became more satisfied with their incomes once they could confirm that pay was distributed fairly.
the difference in happiness between Norwegians with higher and lower incomes grew larger.
items.explanation: Under income comparison models, people judge their well-being partly by “comparing their earnings with those of others.” Once incomes could be looked up “in moments,” such comparisons became easy: people with higher incomes would compare favorably and people with lower incomes unfavorably. The result consistent with the models is a wider happiness gap between the two groups, as D says.

A.why_wrong: Easier comparison would make lower earners feel worse, but people with higher incomes would find many who earned less, so the models do not predict lower happiness at every income level.

B.why_wrong: Lower earners comparing themselves with others would mostly see people who earned more, so the models predict that their satisfaction would fall rather than rise.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about whether pay was fair or seen as fair; the models it describes concern how people compare their own earnings with others’.

sources.what: Perez-Truglia 2020, American Economic Review 110(4):1019, The Effects of Income Transparency on Well-Being: in 2001 Norwegian tax records became easily accessible online; using survey data from 1985 to 2013, the higher transparency increased the gap in happiness between richer and poorer individuals by 29% and the life satisfaction gap by 21%, consistent with income comparisons models

items.notes: Area: social science (economics of well-being). S2 hard T3: the comparison model applied to newly visible incomes; the key needs both halves (richer compare up, poorer compare down). Replaces the Duranton road-congestion draft (subject already used by rhetorical synthesis). Distractors: MIX (everyone less happy), REV (poorer happier), CAUSE (fairness).

band7.why: Two steps (the comparison model; visible incomes make richer people feel better off and poorer worse, so the gap widens). A keeps the true half (poorer people less happy) and overreaches to every level, B a reversal, C an off-model motive. Band 6.

items.subtype: T4 explanation: a chemical principle explains why oil jars were dumped rather than reused
items.passage: Monte Testaccio, an artificial hill in Rome, consists almost entirely of fragments of an estimated 53 million amphorae, nearly all of them vessels that had transported olive oil to the city, predominantly from southern Spain. Romans often recycled broken amphorae, pulverizing the fragments into chips for a widely used concrete bound with lime, yet no comparable accumulation of wine or grain amphorae has been identified. One proposed explanation is chemical: oil absorbed into the porous walls of a ceramic vessel reacts with lime to produce soap. Under that explanation, the oil amphorae were most likely discarded rather than recycled because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: wine and grain amphorae already supplied all of the fragments that Rome’s builders needed for their concrete.
concrete made with chips of their oil-soaked walls would have been of poor quality.
the soap that formed inside them would have spoiled any oil later stored in them, making them useless as containers.
they broke into large, curved pieces that could not easily be pounded into the small chips used in concrete.
items.explanation: Broken amphorae were often pulverized into chips for “a widely used concrete bound with lime,” and oil absorbed into a vessel’s walls “reacts with lime to produce soap.” Chips from oil amphorae would therefore have turned part of the concrete into soap and spoiled it, so it made sense to discard them instead, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how many fragments builders needed; the explanation it offers turns on what happens when oil meets lime.

C.why_wrong: Soap forms when oil reacts with lime, which is used in concrete, not inside an empty oil jar; the text also says nothing about reusing the jars to store oil.

D.why_wrong: This is a different, physical explanation; the text asks what follows from the chemical one, and it says nothing about the shape or size of the fragments.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Monte Testaccio: mound of an estimated 53 million amphorae, mostly Dressel 20 olive-oil vessels from Baetica (southern Spain); many amphorae were pounded into chips for opus signinum; no equivalent mound of wine or grain amphorae; one possible reason: oil reacts chemically with lime, a major component of concrete, to form soap, so the concrete would have been unsatisfactory

items.notes: Area: history (Roman archaeology). S2 T4: oil plus lime makes soap, applied to why oil jars were dumped. The 'If this explanation is correct' frame keeps the real rival account (Dressel 20 fragments hard to reduce to chips) wrong as option D. Distractors: CAUSE (supply), MIX (soap in the jar), CAUSE (fragment size).

fixes: options lengthened toward the band-6 norm (11 to 15 words before); D now names the chips used in concrete, a close rival excluded only by the chemical frame; re-solved, B only

band7.why: Two steps (chips go into lime concrete; oil plus lime makes soap, so the concrete fails). D is the real rival account (fragment shape), excluded only by the frame; C right pieces in the wrong place; A a plain OUT. Models are medium items, so it sits at the low end of band 6 even after the options were lengthened.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: plant regrowth on abandoned land linked to a past climate dip
items.passage: Atmospheric carbon dioxide declined by 7 to 10 parts per million during the late 1500s and early 1600s, a period in which global surface temperatures also dipped slightly. Geographer Alexander Koch and colleagues estimate that epidemics introduced by European colonizers killed approximately 90 percent of the Indigenous population of the Americas within a century of 1492, allowing roughly 56 million hectares of previously cultivated land to revert to forest and other vegetation. Since growing plants absorb carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, from the atmosphere, the researchers concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the vegetation that spread across abandoned land in the Americas accounts by itself for the entire decline in carbon dioxide during that period.
the slight drop in global temperatures made conditions in the Americas more favorable for forests to spread onto abandoned farmland.
the population collapse in the Americas likely contributed to the slight cooling that the world experienced at that time.
Indigenous farmers had cleared more land in the century before 1492 than they had in any earlier century.
items.explanation: The deaths allowed about 56 million hectares of cultivated land to regrow, and “growing plants absorb carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, from the atmosphere,” so the regrowth would have lowered the amount of that gas, which fell in a period when “global surface temperatures also dipped slightly.” Linking these steps, the population collapse likely helped bring about that cooling, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text supports regrowth as one cause of the decline, but nothing in it shows that regrowth alone accounts for the whole 7 to 10 parts per million.

B.why_wrong: The text gives the regrowth as a cause of the carbon dioxide decline that accompanied the cooling, not the cooling as a cause of the regrowth; the land regrew because the people who farmed it had died.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no information about how much land Indigenous farmers cleared in different centuries before 1492.

sources.what: Koch, Brierley, Maslin, Lewis 2019, Quaternary Science Reviews, Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492 (abstract): CO2 fell 7 to 10 ppm in the late 1500s and early 1600s, lowering surface air temperatures by 0.15 C; epidemics removed 90% of the Indigenous population; secondary succession on 55.8 Mha of abandoned land sequestered 7.4 Pg C (3.5 ppm), 47 to 67% of the decline with feedbacks

items.notes: Area: natural science (climate, earth system) with history. S2: plants draw down CO2, applied to land abandoned after the Great Dying, then to the cooling (two links). Distractors: EXT (regrowth the sole cause; the source credits it with about half), MIX (cause and effect swapped), CMP (earlier centuries).

fixes: “a greenhouse gas” added so the cooling link rests on the passage rather than outside knowledge (the source abstract ties the CO2 fall to a 0.15 C cooling)

band7.why: Two steps (regrowth drew down a heat-trapping gas; the fall in that gas accompanied the cooling). A overreaches to the sole cause (source: about half), B swaps cause and effect, D a CMP. Band 6.

items.subtype: T4 explanation: a perceptual principle explains the function of light-absorbing plumage
items.passage: During courtship displays, males of several bird-of-paradise species show patches of brilliant color, such as iridescent blue or green, set against areas of extremely dark plumage. Biologist Dakota McCoy and colleagues determined that the barbules of these super black feathers form tilted arrays that scatter incoming light repeatedly until little of it escapes; some reflect as little as 0.05 percent of incident light, far less than ordinary black feathers reflect. Because animals judge a color’s brightness partly by comparing it with its surroundings, the researchers hypothesize that super black plumage ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: increases the amount of light that the colored patches beside it reflect toward a watching female.
helps a male conceal himself from predators during the long periods when he is not displaying.
evolved because females prefer whichever males have feathers that absorb the most light.
makes the adjacent colored patches look more brilliant to an observing female than they otherwise would.
items.explanation: The colored patches are “set against areas of extremely dark plumage,” and animals judge brightness “partly by comparing it with its surroundings.” A patch surrounded by feathers that reflect almost no light would therefore seem especially bright to a watching female, even though the patch itself reflects no more light than before, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The principle in the text concerns how bright a color is judged to be, not how much light it reflects; dark feathers beside a patch do not make the patch itself reflect more light.

B.why_wrong: The text discusses the dark plumage only as part of the courtship display and says nothing about predators.

C.why_wrong: The text ties the dark plumage to how the neighboring colors are perceived, not to any preference females have for light absorption itself.

sources.what: McCoy, Feo, Harvey, Prum 2018, Nature Communications 9:1 (abstract): five birds-of-paradise species have super black plumage with directional reflectance of 0.05 to 0.31%; tilted arrays of highly modified barbules cause multiple scattering; hypothesis that super black plumage evolved through sensory bias to enhance the perceived brilliance of adjacent color patches during courtship display

items.notes: Area: natural science (ornithology, optics). S2 T4: brightness judged against surroundings, applied to color patches beside super black feathers. Distractors: MIX (reflectance vs perceived brilliance), CAUSE (camouflage), CAUSE (preference for absorption).

band7.why: Two steps (brightness judged by contrast; near-total absorption beside a colored patch raises the contrast). A keeps the right patches and breaks the physics-versus-perception link, C a rival selection account, B an OUT. Band 6.

items.subtype: T2 belief: a program design reveals what its makers believed about listeners
items.passage: Psychologists have long observed that people gradually stop noticing a sound that continues without interruption, such as the hum of a ventilation fan. For decades, the Muzak company supplied offices and factories with background music organized under a system called Stimulus Progression: songs were arranged in 15-minute blocks that grew steadily faster in tempo and brassier in instrumentation, a pattern intended to encourage workers to quicken their pace. After each block, however, the music fell silent for 15 minutes. Given the system’s purpose, these silences most likely reflected the company’s assumption that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: workers would grow accustomed to the music and respond less to its rising energy if it never paused.
workers needed quiet periods to concentrate on tasks that the music would otherwise disrupt.
the music encouraged workers to speed up most when each block began slowly and quietly.
the music would be more effective if workers could predict exactly when each block was going to begin.
items.explanation: People “gradually stop noticing a sound that continues without interruption,” and the music was meant “to encourage workers to quicken their pace.” Music that never paused would risk fading into the background and losing that effect, so the silences most likely reflected an assumption that workers would otherwise respond less and less to the music, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text presents the music as a help to workers’ pace, not a disruption; it gives no reason to think the silences were meant to protect concentration from the music.

C.why_wrong: Each block did begin slower and grow faster, but that describes the music within a block; it does not explain why the music stopped for 15 minutes between blocks.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about workers predicting when music would start; the principle it offers concerns sounds that continue without a break.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Muzak: Stimulus Progression programmed music in 15-minute blocks, gradually faster in tempo and louder and brassier, to encourage workers to speed up and maintain productivity; after each 15-minute segment the music fell silent for 15 minutes; company-funded research showed that alternating music with silence limited listener fatigue and made the stimulus effect more effective

items.notes: Area: social science (industrial psychology, music business). S9 hard: design reveals belief; habituation principle plus the silences. Simplified: 'louder and brassier' kept as 'brassier'; the partly technical reasons for the silences are left out of the passage and no option offers a technical reason. Distractors: CAUSE (concentration), MIX (within-block rise), CAUSE (predictability).

band7.why: Two steps (continuous sound gets tuned out; silences break the continuity so the rising blocks keep their effect), habituation premise two sentences before the blank; B a rival motive, C a true block detail misapplied, D an OUT. Low band 6.

items.subtype: X but not Y: leg bone developed but flight-muscle anchor not, so walking before flying
items.passage: In 2017, paleontologist Xiaolin Wang and colleagues described hundreds of fossilized eggs of the pterosaur Hamipterus tianshanensis from a site in China, sixteen of them containing embryonic remains. In an embryo that appeared to be approaching hatching, the femur, or thigh bone, was well developed, whereas the deltopectoral crest of the humerus—a ridge on the upper wing bone to which the flight muscles attach—remained underdeveloped. These findings suggest that newly hatched Hamipterus ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: could take to the air soon after hatching, since their well-developed hind limbs would have helped launch them into flight.
were probably able to get around on the ground for some time before they were able to fly.
could not move about on their own until the bones of their wings had finished developing.
had fully formed wings that were simply too small at first to lift their bodies off the ground.
items.explanation: Near hatching, the leg bone “was well developed,” but the ridge “to which the flight muscles attach” was not. Without a developed anchor for flight muscles, a hatchling probably could not fly, while its legs were ready to use, so it likely moved about on the ground for a while before it could fly, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The hind limbs were well developed, but flight also needs the flight muscles, and the ridge they attach to was not developed, so the evidence points away from early flight.

C.why_wrong: The wing bone was still developing, but the femur, or thigh bone, “was well developed,” so the hatchlings’ legs were ready to use; the evidence suggests they could get around before they could fly, not that they could not move at all.

D.why_wrong: The text does not describe the wings as fully formed or discuss their size; the feature it says was undeveloped is the ridge where the flight muscles attach.

sources.what: Science News on Wang et al. 2017 (Science 358:1197): hundreds of Hamipterus eggs, 16 with embryos; the deltopectoral crest, where flight muscles attach, was underdeveloped even in an embryo thought close to hatching, while the femur was well developed; hatchlings could walk but not yet fly (an outside researcher urged caution)

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). S6: femur developed but flight-muscle crest not, so walking before flight. Key hedged ('probably') as the source urges caution. No option mentions parental care (the researchers' further suggestion), so no second defensible answer. Distractors: MIX (legs launch flight), REV (immobile until the wing bones finish; review rebuilt this from a CMP), MIX (wing size).

fixes: C (a comparison with other species, killed by one unmeasured comparison) rebuilt as a reversal that keeps the true wing-bone fact (no movement until the wing bones finish); re-solved, B only

band7.why: One to two steps (legs ready, flight-muscle anchor not), like the S6 hard models. A keeps the true hind-limb fact, C the true wing-bone fact, D the true no-flight-at-first point, each breaking one link. Band 6.

items.subtype: T2 belief: counterevidence shows what a theory wrongly assumes
items.passage: Speakers occasionally feel confident that they know a word yet cannot retrieve it, a phenomenon called a “tip of the tongue” state, but some theories of sign language maintain that a sign’s meaning and its form are not stored separately in memory and therefore predict that signers should never experience a comparable state. Psychologist Robin Thompson and colleagues, however, found that deaf users of American Sign Language experienced “tip of the fingers” states, during which they were more likely to recall a sign’s handshape or location than its movement. These findings imply that the theories described ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: would have been supported had signers recalled a sign’s movement more readily than its handshape or location.
are mistaken about signed languages but correctly describe spoken ones, in which a word’s meaning and form are stored as one unit.
underestimate how often signers forget what a familiar sign means while still recalling its handshape or location.
wrongly assume that a signer who has a sign’s meaning in mind will also have access to its form.
items.explanation: The theories hold that a sign’s “meaning and its form are not stored separately in memory” and so “predict that signers should never experience a comparable state.” Yet Thompson’s team found “tip of the fingers” states, in which signers are sure which sign they want but cannot fully produce it, recalling only parts of it such as its handshape or location. A sign’s meaning can therefore be in mind while its form is not, which implies that the theories wrongly assume the two always come together, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The theories predict that signers “should never experience a comparable state,” so any tip of the fingers state counts against them, whichever part of a sign the signer recalls; recalling movement first would not have supported them.

B.why_wrong: The theories described concern sign language, and the text says speakers also have “tip of the tongue” states, feeling confident that they know a word yet unable to retrieve it, so spoken words do not show meaning and form stored as one unit either.

C.why_wrong: In a tip of the fingers state the signer is sure of the sign but cannot fully produce its form; nothing in the text suggests that signers forget what signs mean.

sources.what: Thompson, Emmorey, Gollan 2005, Psychological Science 16:856 (abstract): some theories collapse semantics and phonology in sign language and predict that TOFs should not occur; TOFs were elicited; signers were more likely to retrieve a target sign's handshape, location, and orientation than its movement; supports a division between semantics and phonology in ASL

items.notes: Area: social science (psycholinguistics). S11 hard in the 3.10 frame (what a view implies): theory says meaning and form are one, TOF states show meaning without full form, so the theory is wrong. Review rebuild: key paraphrased (meaning in mind assumed to bring the form); distractors MIX (direction trap: which part is recalled does not matter), EXT (spoken words, ruled out by the tip of the tongue premise), REV (forgetting meaning).

fixes: read easier than band 6 (key restated the theory’s premise plus “wrongly”; A and B each killed by one stated fact): key paraphrased (a signer with the meaning in mind is assumed to have the form), A rebuilt as a direction trap (movement recalled first), B as an overreach to spoken words that the tip of the tongue premise rules out, C kept; explanation and why_wrong rewritten; re-solved, D only
“feel certain” changed to “feel confident” to keep the hard tier’s long-word share at the official level after the other edits

band7.why: After the rebuild: two steps (the theories tie meaning to form; a tip of the fingers state is meaning without full form). A a direction trap on the handshape data, B an overreach the first-sentence tip of the tongue premise rules out, C a reversal of what the state is; key paraphrased. Band 6.

items.subtype: Comparison by leader age applied forward: what losing old leaders would cost
items.passage: Male lions pose an especially severe danger to African elephants. To investigate how elephant families assess such threats, behavioral ecologist Karen McComb and colleagues played recorded lion roars to wild family groups, each led by an older female, known as the matriarch, whose lead the family generally follows. All the families responded more defensively to roars from three lions than to roars from one, but responses to the sex of the roaring lions varied with the matriarch’s age: families with the oldest matriarchs reacted most strongly to male roars, whereas families with younger matriarchs typically under-reacted to them despite the danger males represent. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: younger matriarchs are unable to distinguish the roars of male lions from those of female lions.
families led by younger matriarchs respond weakly to male lions’ roars because they cannot judge how many lions are roaring.
a family that loses its oldest female may be slower to recognize its most dangerous predators.
families led by older matriarchs encounter male lions more often than other families do.
items.explanation: Families with the oldest matriarchs “reacted most strongly to male roars,” while those with younger matriarchs “typically under-reacted to them despite the danger males represent.” Because the family follows the matriarch’s lead, a family that lost its oldest female and came to be led by a younger one would likely respond less to the threat male lions pose, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Families with younger matriarchs “typically under-reacted” to male roars, which shows a weaker response, not an inability to tell male roars from female ones.

B.why_wrong: Families with younger matriarchs did under-react to male roars, but not for lack of a sense of numbers: “All the families responded more defensively to roars from three lions than to roars from one.”

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how often families meet male lions; the study compared responses to recorded roars.

sources.what: McComb, Shannon, Durant, Sayialel, Slotow, Poole, Moss 2011, Proc. R. Soc. B 278:3270 (abstract): playback of lion roars; groups consistently adjust defensive behavior to three roaring lions versus one; families with younger matriarchs typically under-react to roars from male lions despite the severe danger they represent; sensitivity increases with matriarch age

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S1 hard: groups differ by matriarch age, with the number-of-lions result common to all; the key applies the age effect forward (T3). Distractors: EXT (cannot distinguish), MIX (true under-reaction given a wrong cause, the number of lions; review rebuild), CAUSE (more encounters).

fixes: B (wrong variable, killed by the three-versus-one sentence alone) rebuilt with a true first part and a wrong cause (weak response to male roars blamed on judging numbers); re-solved, C only

band7.why: After the rebuild: two steps (the oldest matriarchs read male roars best; the family follows the matriarch, so losing her slows recognition). A an EXT, B a true under-reaction given a wrong cause (numbers, which all families judged), D a rival exposure cause. Band 6.

items.subtype: Dated sources plus misreadings reject a claimed fifteenth-century date
items.passage: In the 1760s, Bristol teenager Thomas Chatterton circulated poems that he attributed to Thomas Rowley, a fifteenth-century monk, saying that the manuscripts had been found in an old chest in a local church. The few “originals” he showed were written on genuinely old parchment. Many antiquarians accepted the poems as medieval, but philologist Walter Skeat later determined that most of the poems’ archaic-looking words are not genuine old words used correctly and that some carry meanings that arose from misreadings of entries in English dictionaries published in 1708 and 1737. Skeat’s findings therefore suggest that the poems ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were most likely composed no earlier than the 1700s, long after Rowley was supposed to have lived.
were genuine fifteenth-century works, since the few originals that Chatterton showed were written on parchment that was truly old.
were written in 1708 or 1737, the years in which the dictionaries containing the misread entries were published.
drew their unusual word meanings from medieval sources that the compilers of those dictionaries had also consulted.
items.explanation: Skeat found that some of the poems’ words “carry meanings that arose from misreadings of entries in English dictionaries published in 1708 and 1737.” An entry can be misread only after the dictionary containing it exists, so the poems could not have been composed before the 1700s, centuries after the “fifteenth-century monk” said to have written them, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The originals were “written on genuinely old parchment,” but the parchment shows only the age of the material; the words written on it carry meanings that “arose from misreadings” of dictionaries from 1708 and 1737, so the text is far younger.

C.why_wrong: The dictionaries’ publication years are only the earliest possible dates for poems that misread them; nothing in the text places the writing of the poems in either of those years.

D.why_wrong: Meanings that “arose from misreadings of entries” in the dictionaries cannot have come from medieval sources, and Skeat found that most of the archaic-looking words “are not genuine old words used correctly.”

sources.what: Maurice Evan Hare, introduction to The Rowley Poems (1911, Project Gutenberg 13037): Chatterton produced poetry that passed for fifteenth century with many antiquaries; he told a friend in 1764 that his old manuscripts had been found in a chest in Redcliffe Church; the few Rowley documents he showed as originals were no doubt written on blank pieces of old parchment from the church chests; he built an antique lexicon from Speght’s Chaucer glossary and the dictionaries of Kersey (1708) and Bailey (1737 edition), often misreading them; Skeat estimates only seven percent of the words in Milles’ glossary are genuine old words correctly used, and notes words given meanings they never bore (Bailey’s Teres major read as tere, a muscle)

Wikipedia, Thomas Chatterton: passed off his work as that of a fictional fifteenth-century poet, Thomas Rowley; Rowleian jargon chiefly from Kersey’s Dictionarium Anglo-Britannicum; language and style analysed by W. W. Skeat (1871)

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, literary forgery). S3 hard (anachronism): words misread from dictionaries of 1708 and 1737 cannot appear in a fifteenth-century text, so the poems date from the 1700s at the earliest; the parchment’s real age sits in its own sentence as a trap. Key hedged (“most likely”). Distractors: REV (old parchment, true, taken as proof), MIX (publication year taken as the date of writing), CAUSE rescue (dictionaries and poems share medieval sources, ruled out by the misreadings). Written by the w4 reviewer to replace the Madeira mice draft, which repeated official rhetorical_synthesis 296801d2.

fixes: replaced: the Madeira mouse-bone draft (Rando et al. 2014) repeated official rhetorical_synthesis 296801d2 (Azores house mice show people arrived before the Portuguese; that item’s option B is this draft’s key); new subject Thomas Chatterton’s Rowley poems and Skeat’s finding that their archaic words come from misread dictionaries of 1708 and 1737 (Hare’s 1911 introduction, Gutenberg 13037); the replacement was written by the reviewer and has had no independent blind solve
review.note: blind answer A was for the replaced Madeira draft (key A, agreed); the new Chatterton item keeps the A key

band7.why: Two steps (an entry can be misread only after its dictionary exists, so 1700s at the earliest; that rules out a fifteenth-century monk), with the parchment trap in its own sentence. B a true parchment fact taken as proof, C the publication years taken as the writing date, D a rescue the misreadings exclude. Band 6.

items.subtype: Two regions, opposite outcomes, so the benefit depends on location
items.passage: Planting forests is frequently promoted as a strategy for slowing global warming, since growing trees remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. But forests influence climate in additional ways: they release water vapor that cools the surrounding air, and their dark canopies absorb considerably more sunlight than open ground does. Using a global climate model to simulate the removal of forests at different latitudes, Govindasamy Bala and colleagues concluded that planting forests in the tropics would clearly help mitigate warming, whereas planting them at high latitudes would be counterproductive. These results suggest that the climate benefit of planting forests ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: depends on the age of the trees, since young forests absorb carbon dioxide more rapidly than mature forests do.
depends on the region, since in some places the warming caused by dark canopies can outweigh the cooling from the carbon dioxide that trees absorb.
is limited to the tropics, since planting forests anywhere else would make warming worse.
comes mainly from the water vapor that trees release rather than from the carbon dioxide they absorb.
items.explanation: Forests cool the climate by taking up carbon dioxide, but “their dark canopies absorb considerably more sunlight than open ground does.” Since new forests would “clearly help” in the tropics yet be “counterproductive” at high latitudes, where trees still absorb carbon dioxide, the warming from their canopies must outweigh that cooling in some regions. So the benefit depends on where the trees are planted, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The study compared forests at different latitudes; the text says nothing about the age of the trees or how fast forests of different ages absorb carbon dioxide.

C.why_wrong: The text reports results only for the tropics and high latitudes; it gives no basis for saying that forests in every other region, such as the middle latitudes, would make warming worse.

D.why_wrong: The text names water vapor as one of several effects but never compares its size with that of carbon dioxide uptake.

sources.what: Bala, Caldeira, Wickett, Phillips, Lobell, Delire, Mirin 2007, PNAS 104:6550 (abstract): biophysical effects of forests (albedo, evapotranspiration, clouds) also affect climate; latitude-specific deforestation experiments in a coupled carbon-climate model indicate afforestation in the tropics would be clearly beneficial in mitigating warming but counterproductive at high latitudes

items.notes: Area: natural science (climate). S7 hard (3.14 pattern): opposite outcomes by region, so the benefit depends on location; the key also needs the albedo step (canopy warming outweighs carbon cooling where the net effect is warming). Simplified: the temperate result (marginal benefit) is left out; option C says 'anywhere else', unsupported either way by the text. Distractors: VAR (tree age), EXT (tropics only), CMP (water vapor vs carbon).

band7.why: Two steps (dark canopies absorb sunlight; at high latitudes that warming outweighs the carbon benefit, so the benefit depends on region). C overreaches from two latitudes to everywhere, D keeps the true water-vapor effect and makes it the main one, A an OUT. Band 6.

items.subtype: Received view (panic or prior bonds) revised by survivor interviews
items.passage: Accounts of crowds in emergencies such as fires or sinking ships have often described “mass panic,” in which each person flees selfishly, or have credited whatever helping occurs to bonds among relatives and friends who were together beforehand. Social psychologist John Drury and colleagues interviewed 21 survivors of 11 emergencies. They found that survivors who felt a strong sense of shared identity with the people around them reported more helping and less panic, and that this shared identity often arose from the emergency itself. These interviews suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: helping during emergencies is explained mainly by bonds that crowd members formed before the emergency began.
strangers caught together in an emergency may cooperate rather than each acting only in their own interest.
survivors who felt a shared identity with those around them had usually known one another before the emergency.
crowds in emergencies are more likely to panic when most of their members are strangers to one another.
items.explanation: Survivors with “a strong sense of shared identity” with those around them reported “more helping and less panic,” and this identity “often arose from the emergency itself.” So people need not know one another beforehand to help each other, which suggests that strangers in an emergency may cooperate instead of fleeing selfishly, as B says.

A.why_wrong: This is the earlier account the study challenges; the shared identity linked to helping “often arose from the emergency itself,” not from earlier bonds.

C.why_wrong: The text says the shared identity often arose from the emergency itself, which points away from the survivors having known one another beforehand.

D.why_wrong: The findings tie less panic to a shared identity that could form during the emergency, so they give no support for expecting crowds of strangers to panic more.

sources.what: Drury, Cocking, Reicher 2009, British Journal of Social Psychology 48:487 (abstract): crowd behaviour in emergencies previously explained by mass panic or pre-existing social bonds; interviews with 21 survivors of 11 emergencies; shared identity enhances solidarity and reduces panic, and such identity can arise from the shared experience of the emergency itself

items.notes: Area: social science (social psychology). S11 medium: two received accounts (panic, prior bonds) and interview evidence. Distractors: REV (old view), MIX (timing of the shared identity), REV (strangers panic more).

items.subtype: Received view (hearing loss inevitable with age) revised by owl hearing tests
items.passage: Hearing loss is widely regarded as an inevitable consequence of aging: in humans and many other mammals, the sensory hair cells of the inner ear are gradually lost and never replaced, although birds can regenerate these cells. Testing barn owls with a behavioral task, biologist Bianca Krumm and colleagues found no significant difference in hearing sensitivity between owls younger than 2 years and owls older than 13, and one owl tested repeatedly over 21 years showed only a slight decline. This finding suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: barn owls hear high-pitched sounds better than mammals of a similar age do.
the hearing of barn owls becomes sharper as the birds grow older.
barn owls lose their sensory hair cells more slowly than mammals lose theirs.
the decline in hearing that often accompanies aging may not be unavoidable for all animals.
items.explanation: Hearing loss is “widely regarded as an inevitable consequence of aging,” yet owls older than 13 heard about as well as owls younger than 2, and one owl “showed only a slight decline” over 21 years. This suggests that losing one’s hearing with age may not be unavoidable for every animal, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The study compared owls of different ages with one another; it did not compare owls’ hearing of high-pitched sounds with that of mammals.

B.why_wrong: The text reports no significant difference between young and old owls and a slight decline in one owl, not hearing that improves with age.

C.why_wrong: The text says birds “can regenerate these cells,” which points to lost cells being replaced, not to cells being lost more slowly.

sources.what: Krumm, Klump, Koppl, Langemann 2017, Proc. R. Soc. B 284:20171584, Barn owls have ageless ears (abstract): behavioural audiograms of owls younger than 2 years and older than 13 years; age group had no significant effect; repeated estimates over 21 years from one individual showed only a slight increase in thresholds; birds regenerate hair cells and may be protected from presbycusis

items.notes: Area: natural science (sensory biology). S11 medium: received view of inevitable age-related hearing loss, counterevidence from barn owls. Distractors: CMP (owls vs mammals), EXT (hearing improves), MIX (slower loss instead of regeneration).

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a conservation principle applied to a donor's display rule
items.passage: Exposure to light damages watercolors, and the deterioration accumulates and cannot be reversed; blues and greens, the pigments frequently used for skies, are typically the first to fade. When collector Henry Vaughan bequeathed 38 watercolors by the English landscape painter Joseph Mallord William Turner to the National Gallery of Scotland in 1900, he stipulated that they be exhibited only in January, the month when daylight is weakest, and stored in darkness for the remainder of the year. Given these conditions, curators would most likely expect that the skies in Vaughan’s watercolors ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: have faded less than those in Turner watercolors displayed year-round in brightly lit rooms.
have faded less than the other parts of the same paintings.
would fade noticeably if the paintings were shown during a single summer month.
were painted with pigments that resist light better than those Turner used in his other works.
items.explanation: Light damage “accumulates and cannot be reversed,” and blues and greens, “the pigments frequently used for skies,” fade first. Vaughan’s watercolors have been shown only in January, “the month when daylight is weakest,” and otherwise kept in darkness, so their skies would have received far less light than those of watercolors shown all year in bright rooms and would likely have faded less, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The blues and greens used for skies “are typically the first to fade,” so within any painting the skies would be expected to fade more than other parts, not less.

C.why_wrong: The text says light damage builds up over time, but it gives no basis for saying that a single month of display would cause noticeable fading.

D.why_wrong: The text attributes the paintings’ protection to the display rule, not to any difference in Turner’s pigments, which it never mentions.

sources.what: Christian Science Monitor, 5 Jan 1996 (Andreae): Vaughan's 38 Turner watercolors, bequeathed in 1900, shown in the month when daylight is weakest and kept in the dark the other 11 months; strong light is destructive to watercolors; damage is cumulative and irreversible; blues and greens used for skies are the most fugitive and fade first; the collection is in particularly fine condition

items.notes: Area: humanities (art conservation, museums). S2 medium: cumulative light damage applied to Vaughan's January-only rule. Distractors: REV (skies fade first, so not less than other parts), EXT (one month noticeable), CAUSE (pigments).

items.subtype: Rule plus observation rejects the premise that amphibians cannot reach oceanic islands
items.passage: Because most amphibians cannot survive prolonged exposure to salt water, they are rarely found on oceanic islands, which emerge from the seafloor and have never been connected to a continent. São Tomé, a volcanic island in the Gulf of Guinea off the coast of West Africa, is one such island, yet it supports Ptychadena newtoni, a frog found nowhere else. Using genetic evidence, biologist John Measey and colleagues confirmed that the frog is a distinct endemic species rather than one introduced by humans. Therefore, the researchers concluded that the frog’s ancestors ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were most likely carried to São Tomé aboard ships by the island’s early settlers.
lived on São Tomé during a period when it was still connected to mainland Africa.
crossed the sea to the island without any help from people.
could tolerate salt water as well as many marine animals can.
items.explanation: São Tomé has “never been connected to a continent,” so the frog’s ancestors could not have walked there, and the genetic evidence shows the frog is not “one introduced by humans.” The only route left is that they crossed the sea on their own, despite amphibians’ usual intolerance of salt water, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The genetic evidence showed that the frog is a distinct species “rather than one introduced by humans,” so the researchers rejected transport by settlers.

B.why_wrong: The text says oceanic islands such as São Tomé “have never been connected to a continent,” so there was no such period.

D.why_wrong: The frogs’ ancestors must have crossed the sea somehow, but nothing in the text suggests that they tolerated salt water as well as marine animals do; the text says most amphibians cannot survive prolonged exposure to it.

sources.what: Measey, Vences, Drewes, Chiari, Melo, Bourles 2007, Journal of Biogeography 34:7, Freshwater paths across the ocean (abstract via Crossref): amphibians are salt-intolerant; Sao Tome and Principe are truly oceanic Gulf of Guinea islands; mtDNA supports the endemic status of Ptychadena newtoni; anthropogenic introduction refuted in favour of natural dispersal (rafting with favourable currents and lowered surface salinity proposed)

items.notes: Area: natural science (biogeography). S3 medium: salt intolerance and an island never joined to land, against an endemic frog not brought by people, so natural sea crossing. Distractors: REV (settlers), REV (land bridge), EXT (marine-level salt tolerance).

items.subtype: Undercut: a confound in the comparison leaves the claim unestablished
items.passage: Clearview is a typeface developed to make highway signs more legible than signs printed in the lettering traditionally used on American highways. Preliminary evaluations found that Clearview signs were between 2 and 8 percent more legible than signs in the traditional lettering, during both daytime and nighttime viewing. However, those evaluations compared newly manufactured Clearview signs with signs already installed along roads, many of which had deteriorated after years of weathering. Therefore, the preliminary evaluations ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: indicate that signs in the traditional lettering are more difficult to read at night than during the day.
suggest that a sign’s lettering affects its legibility more than the sign’s age and condition do.
prove that Clearview signs become harder to read than older signs once they have weathered.
cannot show whether the typeface or the signs’ newer condition made the difference.
items.explanation: The evaluations compared “newly manufactured Clearview signs” with installed signs, “many of which had deteriorated after years of weathering.” Because the Clearview signs differed from the others both in typeface and in condition, the higher legibility could come from either, so the evaluations cannot show which one was responsible, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports that Clearview signs did better “during both daytime and nighttime viewing,” but it never compares how readable the older signs were at night with how readable they were by day.

B.why_wrong: Because the new signs were also in better condition, the evaluations cannot separate the effect of lettering from the effect of age and condition, let alone show that lettering matters more.

C.why_wrong: The evaluations tested new Clearview signs only; they give no information about how Clearview signs perform once they have weathered.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Clearview (typeface): early testing found Clearview two to eight percent more legible in day and night viewing, but the tests compared new Clearview signs to existing, weathered signs in the prior typeface; one source suggested the gain was more due to old, worn signs being replaced with new ones

items.notes: Area: humanities (typography, design) with transport policy. S5 medium: a confound (new vs weathered signs) undercuts the legibility claim, as in 2.11 and 2.18. Distractors: OUT (day vs night for old signs), REV (lettering matters more), EXT (weathered Clearview).

items.subtype: Time sequence: a dated find sets an earlier bound on when a practice began
items.passage: Tobacco is native to the Americas, but until recently the earliest firm evidence of its use by people was nicotine residue in an Alabama pipe approximately 3,300 years old. At the Wishbone site in Utah’s Great Salt Lake Desert, archaeologist Daron Duke and colleagues excavated a hearth used by some of the region’s earliest inhabitants, and among the charred plant remains inside it were four burned seeds of wild tobacco. The seeds themselves were too small to be dated directly, but radiocarbon analysis of other material from the hearth indicated that the fire had burned approximately 12,300 years ago. Duke’s team therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: people in North America were using tobacco thousands of years earlier than the Alabama pipe had indicated.
tobacco was first cultivated as a crop near the Wishbone site approximately 12,300 years ago.
the Alabama pipe is probably considerably older than the 3,300 years that researchers had estimated.
tobacco was used more widely 12,300 years ago than it was 3,300 years ago.
items.explanation: The tobacco seeds were burned in a hearth whose fire “had burned approximately 12,300 years ago,” while the earlier evidence, the Alabama pipe, was “approximately 3,300 years old.” So people were already using tobacco about 9,000 years before the pipe was made, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The seeds came from “wild tobacco,” and the text says nothing about cultivation, so the find shows use of the plant, not farming of it.

C.recipe: date moved to the wrong object (MIX)
C.why_wrong: The new date belongs to the hearth at the Wishbone site; nothing in the text calls into question the age of the Alabama pipe.

D.why_wrong: The text reports single finds from two periods and gives no information about how widely tobacco was used in either.

sources.what: Duke, Wohlgemuth, Adams, Armstrong-Ingram, Rice, Young, Nature Human Behaviour 6:183 (online 2021): excavations at the Wishbone site in North America's desert west uncovered evidence of human tobacco use about 12,300 years ago, 9,000 years earlier than previously documented (news reports: four charred wild tobacco seeds in a hearth in Utah's Great Salt Lake Desert; seeds too small to date, hearth dated; previous record a 3,300-year-old pipe from Alabama)

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S7 medium (2.8 pattern, an onset bound from a dated find). Secondary details (four seeds, Alabama pipe, hearth dated instead of seeds) from news coverage of the paper (e.g., https://www.ksl.com/article/50259992/hearth-site-in-utah-desert-reveals-human-tobacco-use-12300-years-ago). Distractors: EXT (cultivation), MIX (redates the pipe), CMP (wider use).

items.subtype: Elimination: bear ruled out, known hominin ruled out, so a second hominin
items.passage: In 1978, researchers at Laetoli, Tanzania, uncovered 3.66-million-year-old footprints at site G that are widely accepted as the oldest unequivocal evidence of upright walking in the human lineage. A trackway found two years earlier at nearby site A was largely disregarded because it shared curious features with the prints of bears. In 2019, anthropologist Ellison McNutt and colleagues reexcavated the site A trackway and compared it with tracks of black bears, chimpanzees, and humans: the prints resembled hominin prints more than bear prints, yet their foot proportions and gait differed clearly from those of the site G prints. Thus, the researchers concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the site A prints were probably made by a bear whose gait differed from that of modern black bears.
at least two kinds of hominins with different ways of walking were present at Laetoli.
the site G prints may not have been made by a hominin after all.
the site A prints must be considerably older than those at site G.
items.explanation: The site A prints “resembled hominin prints more than bear prints,” which rules out a bear, but their “foot proportions and gait differed clearly from those of the site G prints,” which rules out the hominin that left the site G tracks. A second kind of hominin, walking differently, must therefore have been at Laetoli, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The comparison showed that the site A prints “resembled hominin prints more than bear prints,” so the researchers set the bear explanation aside.

C.recipe: doubt moved to the wrong site (MIX)
C.why_wrong: The site G prints are “widely accepted” as hominin evidence, and the study questioned nothing about them; it was the site A prints whose maker was in doubt.

D.why_wrong: The text gives an age only for the site G prints and says nothing about when the site A prints were made.

sources.what: McNutt et al. 2021, Nature 600:468 (abstract): Laetoli site G trackways (3.66 Ma, discovered 1978) are the oldest unequivocal evidence of obligate bipedalism; a site A trackway found two years earlier was marginalized because of curious affinities with bears; in 2019 the team relocated and excavated it and compared it with American black bears, chimpanzees and humans; the prints resemble hominins more than ursids, but foot proportions, gait and 3D morphology differ from site G, indicating at least two hominin taxa

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (paleoanthropology). S4 medium (2.17 pattern): two exclusions, bear and the site G hominin. The key says 'present at Laetoli', not 'at the same time' (the text gives no date for site A). Distractors: REV (bear), MIX (doubt moved to site G), EXT (older).

items.subtype: Co-occurrence of low solar output and fewer hurricanes suggests a link
items.passage: Documentary records of hurricanes in the Caribbean before the twentieth century are fragmentary, making long-term trends difficult to reconstruct. Seeking an alternative source of evidence, climatologist Valerie Trouet and colleagues compiled a record of Spanish ships wrecked in the Caribbean between 1495 and 1825 and combined it with growth records from trees in the Florida Keys, whose growth is suppressed after storms damage them. The researchers found that hurricane activity in the Caribbean declined by approximately 75 percent during the Maunder Minimum (1645–1715), a period in which the Sun emitted unusually little energy. This pattern suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Spanish ships built during the Maunder Minimum were sturdier than those built in earlier periods.
hurricanes will become less frequent in the Caribbean if the Sun’s output declines again in the coming centuries.
variations in the energy emitted by the Sun may be linked to how frequently hurricanes occur in the Caribbean.
hurricanes struck the Caribbean less often during the Maunder Minimum than they struck other regions.
items.explanation: Hurricane activity in the Caribbean fell by “approximately 75 percent” during the Maunder Minimum, “a period in which the Sun emitted unusually little energy.” Because the drop in storms coincided with the drop in the Sun’s output, the findings suggest that the two may be connected, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text treats the shipwrecks as a record of storms and gives no information about how the ships were built; the tree records, too, point to fewer storms.

B.why_wrong: The text describes a single past period in which the two declines coincided; it does not support a firm prediction about storms in the coming centuries.

D.why_wrong: The study examined the Caribbean only, so the text gives no basis for comparing it with other regions.

sources.what: Trouet, Harley, Dominguez-Delmas 2016, PNAS 113:3169 (abstract): limited observational records; a documentary series of Spanish shipwrecks in the Caribbean (1495-1825) combined with a tree-growth suppression chronology from the Florida Keys (1707-2009); a 75% reduction in decadal-scale Caribbean tropical cyclone activity during the Maunder Minimum (1645-1715), the most severe reduction in solar irradiance in documented history

items.notes: Area: history with climate science. S8 medium: a drop in storms coinciding with low solar output suggests a link (hedged 'may be linked'; the source names ocean and atmosphere patterns as the route). Distractors: CAUSE (sturdier ships), FUT (firm prediction), CMP (other regions).

items.subtype: X but not Y: behavior changed inside the activity but not outside it
items.passage: Political scientist Salma Mousa randomly assigned Iraqi Christians displaced by the Islamic State to soccer teams that were either exclusively Christian or integrated with Muslim players. Christians with Muslim teammates were subsequently more likely to vote for a Muslim player from another team to receive a sportsmanship award and, six months after the intervention, to train alongside Muslims. Nevertheless, they were no more likely than other participants to patronize a restaurant in Muslim-majority Mosul or to attend a mixed social event. Mousa therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: contact through a shared activity may change behavior within that activity more readily than behavior elsewhere.
playing alongside Muslims made the Christian participants less willing to interact with Muslims outside of soccer.
the Christian participants’ attitudes toward Muslims had become entirely positive by the end of the season.
soccer is more effective than other team sports at building trust between members of different groups.
items.explanation: Christians on mixed teams treated Muslims differently within soccer, voting for a Muslim player for an award and later choosing “to train alongside Muslims,” but they were “no more likely than other participants” to visit a restaurant in Mosul or attend a mixed social event. The contact changed behavior inside the shared activity more than outside it, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says the Christians on mixed teams were “no more likely” than others to engage with Muslims outside soccer, not that they became less willing.

C.why_wrong: The study measured specific behaviors, and the lack of change outside soccer gives no basis for claiming entirely positive attitudes.

D.why_wrong: The study involved only soccer, so the text cannot support a comparison with other team sports.

sources.what: Mousa 2020, Science 369:866 (abstract): Iraqi Christians displaced by ISIS randomly assigned to all-Christian or mixed teams; Christians with Muslim teammates more likely to vote for a Muslim (not on their team) for a sportsmanship award, register for a mixed team, and train with Muslims 6 months after the intervention; no substantial effect on patronizing a restaurant in Muslim-dominated Mosul or attending a mixed social event

items.notes: Area: social science (political science, intergroup contact). S6 medium: changes within soccer but not outside it. Distractors: REV (less willing), EXT (entirely positive attitudes), CMP (other sports).

items.subtype: Content reveals purpose: a fake entry as a trap for copiers
items.passage: The 1975 edition of the New Columbia Encyclopedia included an entry on Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fountain designer turned photographer who died in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine. No such person ever existed; the editors had invented her on purpose. Writing an encyclopedia takes years of work, and a rival publisher could copy the entries and sell them as its own. The editors most likely included the fake entry because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: they wanted to reward careful readers with a joke hidden among the serious entries.
it would reveal whether another book had copied their entries.
they had too little information about Mountweazel’s photographs to describe them in detail.
the encyclopedia needed more entries about photographers than its writers had time to research.
items.explanation: The text says a rival publisher “could copy the entries and sell them as its own.” Since Mountweazel never existed, no honest writer would know about her, so if her entry showed up in another book, it would prove that the book had been copied. That is why the editors most likely added it, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The entry is amusing, but the text points instead to the risk that a rival publisher could copy the entries, and a made-up entry is what would expose such copying.

C.why_wrong: Mountweazel was invented, so there were no real photographs to describe; the editors made up her details on purpose.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about a need for more entries on photographers; the fake entry was invented on purpose, not added to fill a gap.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Fictitious entry: Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a fictitious biographical entry intentionally placed as a copyright trap in the 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia; a fountain designer turned photographer who died in an explosion while on assignment for Combustibles magazine; fictitious entries are added as copyright traps to reveal later plagiarism

items.notes: Area: humanities (reference publishing). S9 easy (1.8 and 1.11 pattern): the fake entry reveals the editors' purpose. Distractors: CAUSE (a joke), REV (missing information), OUT (more entries).

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a warning followed applied to a later tsunami
items.passage: In the coastal village of Aneyoshi, Japan, a stone tablet stands beside the road that climbs from the sea. Villagers who had lived through earlier tsunamis put it up, and its inscription warns, “Do not build your homes below this point!” Since then, residents have kept their houses on the higher ground above the stone. In many other Japanese communities, however, similar stones were disregarded as towns expanded toward the shoreline after World War II. When a huge tsunami struck the northeastern coastline in 2011, its waves stopped about 300 feet below the Aneyoshi stone. This suggests that by following the stone’s warning, the people of Aneyoshi most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: kept the 2011 waves from rising any higher than the stone.
received an early warning that the 2011 tsunami was coming.
persuaded other towns to move their homes away from the shore.
kept their homes out of reach of the 2011 tsunami.
items.explanation: Residents have kept their houses “on the higher ground above the stone,” and in 2011 the waves “stopped about 300 feet below the Aneyoshi stone.” Because the water never reached the stone, it could not have reached the homes built above it, so following the warning most likely kept those homes safe, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The stone is a warning, not a barrier; the waves stopped below it on their own, and the villagers’ choice affected where their homes stood, not how high the water rose.

B.why_wrong: The stone warns people where not to build; the text says nothing about anyone receiving advance notice that the 2011 tsunami was coming.

C.why_wrong: The text says that in many other communities similar stones were disregarded as towns expanded toward the shoreline, not that Aneyoshi persuaded them to move.

sources.what: NBC News (AP/NYT report, April 2011): the Aneyoshi stone warns 'Do not build your homes below this point!'; villagers who knew the horrors of tsunamis erected it; the 2011 waves stopped just 300 feet below the stone; more commonly such stones were disregarded as coastal towns grew after World War II

items.notes: Area: history (disaster history, Japan). S2 easy: a building rule applied to the 2011 tsunami. Distractors: REV (stone stopped waves), OUT (early warning), REV (persuaded other towns).

items.subtype: Two outcomes of one event lead to a mixed conclusion
items.passage: Winning a major literary prize is usually considered good news for a novel. Researchers Balázs Kovács and Amanda Sharkey tested this assumption using thousands of reader reviews on the website Goodreads. They studied 64 English-language books that had either won a prestigious award or been named a finalist between 2007 and 2011. After the winners were announced, the winning books attracted more new readers than the finalists did. But readers’ ratings of the winning books also declined more sharply than ratings of the finalists did. The researchers suggest that a prize attracts readers whose tastes may not suit the book. They add that some readers may be discouraged by a book’s sudden popularity. Hence, winning a prize may ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: lead publishers to print fewer copies of books that were only finalists.
cause readers who loved a book before it won to stop recommending it to others.
help a book reach more readers while lowering what readers think of it.
matter more to a book’s sales than the quality of its writing does.
items.explanation: After the announcement, the winning books “attracted more new readers than the finalists did,” but their ratings “declined more sharply than ratings of the finalists did.” A prize can therefore bring a book a larger audience while also lowering how that audience rates it, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how many copies publishers print of any book.

B.why_wrong: The text suggests some readers may be discouraged by a book’s popularity, but it says nothing about earlier fans stopping their recommendations.

D.why_wrong: The study compared winners with finalists; it did not weigh prizes against the quality of a book’s writing.

sources.what: Kovacs and Sharkey 2014, Administrative Science Quarterly 59:1, The Paradox of Publicity (abstract): Goodreads reviews of 64 English-language books that won or were short-listed for prestigious awards in 2007-2011; prizewinning books attract more readers after the announcement, and their ratings decline more than those of finalists; explained by an audience with more diverse tastes and by popularity being off-putting to some

items.notes: Area: humanities and social science (literature, sociology of culture). S7 easy (1.2 pattern): one event, two outcomes, so a mixed effect. Distractors: OUT (print runs), EXT (fans stop recommending), CMP (prize vs writing quality).
